title: Crane Down
description: A crane down shot lowers the camera on an arm from a high wide view into a human-scale frame. The world collapses from map to face because the lens occupies new heights, not because it merely nods.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: Arrive from a god-view into a person without resetting attention. What begins as an overview can become an intimate encounter in one path.

Some famous descents even hand off from crane to ground support and keep walking. It is the wrong tool when you only need to look down from a locked roof, or when a cut from aerial to close-up would be cleaner.
Do not assume every continuous-looking descent was achieved without a join.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Plan the high composition and the human landing. The arm descends, often moving forward as well, with a remote head keeping the subject framed.
If you add a support handoff, match direction, speed, height, and horizon at the transfer. Prompt a crane down from a high wide view into a closer frame, map collapsing to face.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: Use it to arrive from god-view into a person. Concrete beat: a valley of tents, then one volunteer with a bag.
Do not tour on the way down.

sections.title: Compared with similar shots

blocks.text: A Crane Up leaves the person for the map. A Tilt Down only pitches from one height.
A Pedestal Down drops on a column with tilt locked and little or no boom. An Aerial Push In starts higher still, from helicopter or drone altitude.
Crane UpEnd a scene, reveal a city, or turn a person into landscape.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: Bound for Glory descends from a crane in the migrant camp and continues at ground level. Contact's VLA shot descends and continues with Ellie toward a building.
I Am Cuba traverses spaces with extraordinary continuous-looking movement. The Shining and Magnolia also use descending arms as arrival.
Check each shot's joins before claiming a single rig.

sections.title: Prompt it

blocks.text: Crane down onto [Subject], starting high and descending into a human-scale frame, the world collapsing from map to face. For motion: the camera cranes down from a high wide view into a closer frame on [Subject].

Begin high over a lively harbor market. Descend beside a woman unloading oranges, then continue at her shoulder as she walks between stalls. The high-to-ground movement feels continuous with no sudden speed or horizon change. Plan separate crane and walking sections joined at a foreground canopy if needed.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: The usual wrong cousin is a Tilt Down or a cut from aerial to close-up. The tell is a nodding camera that never loses altitude, or a scale jump.
The fix: continuous descent of the station point, matched horizon, a readable human landing.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is Crane Down in film?
It is a physical descent of the camera on a crane or jib from a high view into a closer, human-scale composition.
Crane Down vs Tilt Down
Tilt down looks down from a fixed height. Crane down moves the camera through height, so you actually arrive at the person.
When should I use Crane Down?
When an overview should become an encounter without a cut. Do not use it if you only needed to glance at the floor.
How do I prompt Crane Down for AI image or video?
Write crane down from a high wide view into a closer frame on [Subject], continuous descent, no cut to aerial. Name the landing size.
